Calculate continuous time transition probabilities

tpm_ct.Rd

A continuous-time Markov chain is described by an infinitesimal generator matrix \(Q\). When observing data at time points \(t_1, \dots, t_n\) the transition probabilities between \(t_i\) and \(t_{i+1}\) are calculated as $$\Gamma(\Delta t_i) = \exp(Q \Delta t_i),$$ where \(\exp()\) is the matrix exponential. The mapping \(\Gamma(\Delta t)\) is also called the Markov semigroup. This function calculates all transition matrices based on a given generator and time differences.

Usage

tpm_ct(Q, timediff, rates = NULL, ad = NULL, report = TRUE)

tpm_cont(Q, timediff, rates = NULL, ad = NULL, report = TRUE)

Arguments

Q

infinitesimal generator matrix of the continuous-time Markov chain of dimension c(nStates, nStates), or array of generator matrices of dimension c(nStates, nStates, nObs-1) (or larger) for time-varying generators, e.g. from generator(beta, Z).

timediff

time differences between observations of length nObs-1 when based on nObs observations

rates

optional vector of state-dependent rates for MM(M)PP fitting. For the MM(M)PP likelihood, the matrices needed in the forward algorithm are \(\exp((Q - \Lambda) \Delta t)\), where \(\Lambda\) is a diagonal matrix with the state-dependent rates on the diagonal.

ad

optional logical, indicating whether automatic differentiation with RTMB should be used. By default, the function determines this itself.

report

logical, indicating whether Q should be reported from the fitted model. Defaults to TRUE, but only works if ad = TRUE.

Value

array of continuous-time transition matrices of dimension c(nStates, nStates, nObs-1)

Details

Transition probabilities. The entry \((i,j)\) of \(\Gamma(\Delta t) = \exp(Q \Delta t)\) is the probability that the chain is in state \(j\) at time \(t + \Delta t\), given that it is in state \(i\) at time \(t\). Its rows sum to one. For short intervals, \(\Gamma(\Delta t)\) is close to the identity matrix. For long intervals, each row is close to the stationary distribution (see stationary_ct). This is what makes continuous-time models suitable for irregularly sampled data: each interval gets its own transition matrix.

Time-varying generators. If Q is an array of generator matrices, e.g. from generator(beta, Z), the generator is assumed constant within each interval, and Q[, , t] is used for timediff[t]. Hence, row \(t\) of Z should contain the covariates at the start of interval \(t\), i.e. at observation \(t\). Only the first length(timediff) slices of Q are used.

Repeated time differences. If Q is a single matrix, \(\Gamma(\Delta t)\) only depends on \(\Delta t\). Hence, the matrix exponential is computed only once for each unique value in timediff and then copied to all intervals with that time difference. This happens automatically, so there is no need to do it manually. It saves a lot of time when there are only few unique time differences, e.g. when time is measured in days or observations are regular with occasional gaps. Copying is free on the RTMB tape, and when all time differences are unique, nothing changes.

MM(M)PPs. If rates are provided, the function returns \(\exp((Q - \Lambda) \Delta t)\) with \(\Lambda = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_N)\). Its entry \((i,j)\) is the probability of moving from state \(i\) to state \(j\) over the interval without any arrival in between, so its rows sum to less than one. Multiplied with the state-dependent rates at the arrival times (in allprobs), these matrices give the MM(M)PP likelihood in the forward algorithm.

Computation. Without automatic differentiation, the matrix exponential is calculated in C++ with Armadillo, separately for each interval. With automatic differentiation (ad = TRUE), Matrix::expm is called for each interval, i.e. a Padé approximation with scaling and squaring, all of which is recorded on the RTMB tape.

For two states, a closed form is used in the AD case instead. Let \(A = Q - \Lambda\) (or \(A = Q\) without rates) with real eigenvalues \(\nu_1 > \nu_2\). Then $$\exp(A \Delta t) = e^{\nu_1 \Delta t} I + \frac{e^{\nu_1 \Delta t} - e^{\nu_2 \Delta t}}{\nu_1 - \nu_2} (A - \nu_1 I).$$ Without rates, \(\nu_1 = 0\) and \(\nu_2 = -(q_{12} + q_{21})\), so that, e.g., \(\Gamma_{12}(\Delta t) = q_{12} (1 - e^{-(q_{12} + q_{21}) \Delta t}) / (q_{12} + q_{21})\). This is exact, not an approximation. For two states, models are therefore expected to be much faster to fit (often by more than an order of magnitude for the gradient): the closed form needs only a few elementwise operations on vectors of length length(timediff), whereas Matrix::expm records a full Padé approximation (matrix products, a linear solve and repeated squaring) on the tape separately for each interval, all of which needs to be evaluated and differentiated in every optimisation step.

See also

Other transition probability matrix functions: generator(), generator_g(), tpm(), tpm_emb(), tpm_emb_g(), tpm_g(), tpm_g2(), tpm_p()

Examples

# building a Q matrix for a 3-state cont.-time Markov chain
Q = generator(rep(-2, 6))

# draw random time differences
timediff = rexp(100, 10)

# compute all transition matrices
Gamma = tpm_cont(Q, timediff)
#> tpm_cont() is deprecated, please use tpm_ct() instead.
